correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the defender exchange proof for ordinary domination (closed neighborhoods). Both predicates guarantee initial domination: each vertex outside a shore's selection has an adjacent selected opposite-side vertex, including in the unique-defender case. In line 42 the p=0 swap argument uses initial domination, which forces the entire B shore selected if p=0; thus b_i really is still selected after exchanging b_j for a_i with j≠i. With p≥1 the exchange leaves at least two selected vertices in A, so in either case the B side is safe. On A, after losing a defender, q≥3 leaves at least two selected in B; for q=2, a 00 attack needs a retained defender from a 11 pair, while a 01 attack can retain its own matched B vertex. When q=1 and an A vertex is outside, it must be the sole such vertex and adjacent to the defender, exactly (a,c,d)=(1,0,1); q=0 requires no outside A vertex. Reflecting gives the other predicate. Multinomial counting is valid by labeled pair assignments. At n≥5 and size at most four neither shore can be full, and one selected vertex on a shore would force n−1 on the other; therefore both occupancies must be two and d≥1. The two stated profiles then give the stated minimum-set count. A fresh adjacency-mask replay at /workspace/branches/audit_crown.py checked the predicate and every bivariate coefficient for each n=3,…,8; minimum size and count outputs were (3,14), (4,62), (4,70), (4,135), (4,231), (4,364). Exhaustion on this range checks the implementation and small boundaries, not the infinite proof.

evidence: The complete multipartite polynomial treats ordinary secure domination, but a bipartite crown with a missing matching is not complete multipartite.

The secure-total crown classification rules out balanced occupancy (2,2) for all n≥3. The ordinary criterion allows that occupancy with a selected matched pair. Conversely the restrained crown predicate can admit single matching pairs as size-two sets, which are not ordinary secure dominating; restraint also rejects an entire shore, which is ordinary secure dominating.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A stronger predicate on the same graph does not enumerate the extra ordinary secure sets; unrestricted complete multipartite shore arguments also lose the defining index obstructions.

evidence: On crowns the secure-total rule tests ordinary exchange plus domination of all selected vertices after replacement; that extra demand suppresses the one-remaining-defender cases where the 01/11 information is decisive.

The prism result's identical size-four family for n≥5 accounts for that coefficient only, not the four-state equivalence. No statement in the independently inspected open sources establishes the latter for ordinary secure domination.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Prior overlap is substantial at the level of the object, polynomial methodology, and one coefficient. The retained conclusion distinguishes 00, 01, and 11 states in marginal occupancies and does not follow from any of the inspected analogue statements.

evidence: The complete prism K_n □ K₂ is the complement of a crown graph; the prism result uses secure connected rather than ordinary secure domination. Its classification gives exactly the same balanced size-four sets with a selected matched pair, explaining the equal minimum-set count for n≥5. It does not produce the whole crown classification: two disjoint triples of selected indices on the two shores are crown secure when n≥6 but fail the prism overlap/connectedness condition.
The ordinary secure-domination polynomial of paths is for a different graph family; the 2026 connected-secure polynomial article names paths, cycles, complete graphs, stars and coronas.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Compared the graph both as a matching deletion and by complementation, and distinguished replacement predicates. An ordinary cardinality specialization is weaker than the joint side-size profile.

value.rationale: The result isolates how the deleted matching affects defender exchanges and counts all sets by side sizes, including which rare marginal occupancies can be secure. This is a natural refinement of the scalar invariant on a standard graph family and gives more information than the stricter same-graph analogues or the single shared coefficient with complete prisms.
